tier_reason: The arXiv paper (v1, not peer-reviewed) reports std::unordered_map vs static_maps::unordered_map averages of 89.6 vs 35.8 us, 1746.8 vs 607.6 us and 21228.1 vs 15295.3 us (Fig. 2). Section 2.2.4 states the Intel Core i5-1240P CPU, g++ 15.2.1 and -std=c++23 -O3 -march=native. The figshare deposit publishes the benchmark code: main.cpp (-D STD_UNORDERED_MAP vs -D STATIC_UNORDERED_MAP, with a Makefile), codon_to_amino_acid.cpp and stock_to_price.cpp (-D STD vs -D STATIC). That meets every Tier A condition.

corrections.workload: Construction + lookup runtime per program run, repeated many times and shown as histograms in the paper (the text does not give the run count), on three demos: (1) average isotopic mass lookup by element symbol, with 1024 random lookups per run (main.cpp); (2) translation of 65,536 random codons to amino acids per run (codon_to_amino_acid.cpp); (3) in-place random updates of S&P 500 stock prices by ticker symbol, 64 x number-of-symbols updates per run (stock_to_price.cpp). The std baseline is std::unordered_map<std::string_view, ...> with the default std::hash.
corrections.caveats: The code is a Figshare software deposit (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.31416038, v1 published 2026-02-26), not a live GitHub repo, so there is no commit history or star count. The figshare API lists the three demo sources, an MIT LICENSE, a Makefile for the element demo and a vendored Frozen copy (Apache-2.0). It has no PTHash or gperf harness and no repeat-run script, so the PTHash and gperf numbers cannot be reproduced from the deposit. The timed runtime includes construction: std::unordered_map is built at run time, while static_maps is built at compile time. The compile times are the trade-off: 7.3 s / 2.2 s / 55.2 s for static_maps::unordered_map vs 0.9 s / 0.9 s / 1.5 s for std::unordered_map (Table 1). The paper is an arXiv preprint. The Fig. 2 caption wrongly says map vs std::map, but the panel titles show std::unordered_map and frozen::unordered_map.

notes: All ratios in claimed_speedup match the paper: 35.8/89.6, 607.6/1746.8, 15295.3/21228.1 vs std, and 35.8/44.9, 607.6/1365.5, 15295.3/15804.5 vs Frozen, plus PTHash 104.7 us and gperf 40.6 us on the element demo only. The figshare API (api.figshare.com) is reachable even though the HTML landing page is not. last_commit is the figshare v1 publication date. maintenance_status 'finished' had no author statement behind it, and the paper lists future work. Minor paper inconsistency: it says the i5-1240P has 12 cores and 24 threads, but Intel's spec is 16 threads. baseline_stdlib libstdc++ is inferred from g++ 15.2.1 on Linux and is not stated explicitly.

tier_reason: The README 'Benchmarks (run-time)' tables show mph against std::map, std::unordered_map and gperf. The benchmark code is public (benchmark/benchmark.cpp on the benchmark branch, using nanobench). Compiler names and flags are given (clang++/g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -DNDEBUG -mbmi2), but no compiler versions and no CPU model. That is first-party code with partial methodology, so Tier C.

corrections.workload: Per-lookup latency (nanobench, minEpochIterations 1,000,000) on small string-keyed static maps, with keys drawn uniformly at random from the key set. Key sets: 5 keys of length 4, 5 keys of length 8, 6 keys of length 2-5, 100 keys of length 8, and 100 keys of length 1-8; a 5-key random uint set was measured for mph only. Baselines: std::map, std::unordered_map (with boost::hash), boost::unordered_map, boost::container::flat_map and gperf-generated lookup code. Harness: benchmark/benchmark.cpp and data.hpp on the repo's benchmark branch.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark. The harness is on the benchmark branch, last changed 2024-07-02, so the README numbers may predate the current main code. The README gives compiler names and flags but no compiler versions and no CPU model, so the tier is capped at C. The std::unordered_map baseline uses boost::hash, not std::hash. The largest key set is 100 keys, not 149. mph::hash assumes valid keys, while the map baselines call find() with miss handling. The random_uints_5 row has no baseline. The speedup vs std::unordered_map is about 2.4x-10x across rows (derived from page data), which is plausible for 5-100 key sets.

notes: The claimed numbers match the clang++ table exactly: 5.56 vs 1.61 ns, 15.32 vs 1.58 ns, and gperf 8.04 ns. mph is fastest in every benchmark group under both compilers. Metadata checks out: MIT license (in .github/LICENSE and the header, so spdx is null), 265 stars, last commit 2025-07-20, stale. baseline_stdlib libstdc++ is inferred from the g++ run; the stdlib for the clang++ run is not stated.

tier_reason: The README BENCHMARKS section has first-party tables against gperf, produced by examples/bench.pl, on an Intel Core i5-2300 CPU. The page states no compiler or flags. The code builds with Perl's configured $Config{cc} and $Config{optimize}, rewritten to -O3 (t/test.pl), so the compiler version is unknown. That fits Tier C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On the 99,171-key dictionary, gperf never produced a table: every run was killed ('with -1 errors. (killed)') after 65-386 s of generation. hanovpp/hanov/urban generated in about 0.79-1.73 s, and their full-dictionary lookup runs took 0.0074-0.0161 s (switch: 0.0052-0.0074 s). On the 2,000-key dictionary, lookup is at parity: pearsonnp 0.001418 s, gperf 0.001428 s, urban 0.001508 s, switch 0.001514 s, hanovpp 0.001609 s. gperf's C output compiled slowest there (0.873 s vs 0.084-0.523 s for the other methods). On 127 keys, pearson 0.001178 s and switch 0.001190 s vs gperf 0.001199 s. The win over gperf is scalability and generation time on large key sets, not lookup speed.
corrections.workload: Wall time of running the generated C test executable, which looks up every dictionary key once (process startup included), plus generation time and C compile time. Dictionaries: 99,171 keys (/usr/share/dict/words; four option combinations), 2,000 keys and 127 keys. Compared: hanovpp/hanov/urban/pearson/pearsonnp/cmph-*/switch code generated by Perfect::Hash vs gperf-generated C.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the benchmark page. examples/bench.pl compiles through t/test.pl compile_static: Perl's configured $Config{cc} with $Config{optimize} (-O1/-O2/-Os/-Ox rewritten to -O3) plus ExtUtils::Embed ccflags. Generated C files over 150 MB drop to -O0. The compiler version is unknown.
corrections.caveats: Own benchmark script (examples/bench.pl). The CPU model is stated, but the compiler and flags are not on the page, so Tier C. The '*lookup*' column is the wall time of a whole process, one lookup per key, so it is dominated by process startup at small sizes. Lookup speed is at parity with gperf on 2,000 and 127 keys. The measurable win is that gperf fails, or takes over 65 s and is killed, on about 100k keys, while Perfect::Hash generates in about 1-2 s. The project is a Perl module and CLI (pperf) that emits C code. It bundles cmph-2.0 and bob/nbperf. The README is marked '(alpha)'.

notes: The record wrongly said gperf had the fastest 2,000-key lookup: pearsonnp at 0.001418 s beats it. It also narrowed the compile-time range to 0.08-0.14 s, but the true range is 0.084-0.523 s. This is a real but narrow entry. Consider it borderline on 'faster', because the only clear win is generation scalability and time vs gperf. The metric field says latency, but the real win is build/generation time; metric is not a correctable field. Metadata checks out: license 'same terms as Perl itself' (= Artistic-1.0-Perl OR GPL-1.0-or-later), 79 stars, last commit 2022-05-31, abandoned, not a fork. The language field says C, but the generator is Perl; only its output is C.
